 Earlier sunsets and more time in darkness are caused by Daylight Saving Time, which is having a direct effect on the happiness and productivity of students. Many Americans support doing away with the traditional time change, but before any government action, it is our responsibility to find enjoyment through the winter.

 KRISHNAN: Is daylight saving time ruining our happiness?
 By 
 Avanthi Krishnan 
 Nov 19, 2026, 12:54 AM
 There is something disappointing about leaving your afternoon lecture, only to find out that the sun has already called it a day. Just a few weeks ago, a 5 p.m. evening stroll was a great way to balance the day and soak in the last few hours of sunlight. Now, it means walking back home in the dark, wondering how the day slipped away so quickly. 
 Nov. 1, 2025, marked the end of Daylight Saving Time , when millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep as clocks changed at 2 a.m. Most people enjoy that "extra sleep," but we trade it for something just as valuable: feeling like we have time left in our day. 
 Over the past week, New Brunswick sunsets have been as early as 4:40 p.m. For Rutgers students already balancing exams, extracurriculars, work and social commitments, the timing is not ideal. The main question is: Are earlier sunsets just an inconvenience, or are they really affecting our happiness? Research indicates the answer is more complex than we think. 
 According to the National Institutes of Health , sunlight is an important factor in regulating our mood, affecting the levels of molecules that help maintain proper serotonin levels. Moderate serotonin levels are associated with positive, calm moods, whereas lower levels can cause sadness and poorer sleep quality. These symptoms can cause Seasonal Affective Disorder, with decreased serotonin levels during winter months. A study of nationwide data from the Danish Psychiatric Central Research Register found an 11 percent increase in depressive episodes, following the transition from summertime to Daylight Saving Time. Though this does not confirm that the time change is a direct cause of depression, it does suggest that the seasonal transition can have psychological consequences. 
 For college students, the impact is often worse because many are already away from home and navigating a new chapter on their own. College counselor Paige Spangler says, "Students have created a rhythm to homework and how they accomplish things day to day ... Daylight saving time throws that equilibrium off."
 A survey from Monmouth University backs up how people feel about Daylight Saving Time. Sixty-one percent of Americans want to get rid of the practice of resetting our clocks entirely. Though their reasons are not identified, it is safe to assume mood changes play a large role. Furthermore, 56 percent of Americans prefer a permanent daylight saving time with less light in the morning and more in the evening. Many dislike their days ending early.
 The problem is not that we have fewer hours to get things done. It is that darkness creates the illusion that the day has ended, even when responsibilities have not. In my experience, it is harder to be productive after my classes when the outside environment tells me to go to bed. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine sees these impacts and is advocating for a "permanent standard time."
 But national policy changes are beyond our control. What we can do is change how we respond to this inevitable seasonal shift. Instead of treating our evenings as shorter, or unproductive failures, we can make a conscious effort to prioritize the daylight that we still have. This means taking walks between classes, studying by a window, making outdoor plans earlier in the day and having relaxing indoor activities for cold, dark evenings. I have been loving movie nights, study sessions with friends and baking, even after the sun sets. These actions shift the feeling that our days are "over" at 5 p.m. to the sense that we still have time left.
 Ultimately, Daylight Saving Time does not end happiness altogether. What it does do is make us realize how much we value the sunlight and the role it plays in our daily lives. But this period of lower sunlight does not have to be dreadful. We just have to remember that we can still find enjoyment. The conscious choices we make about what we do and who we are with during these times have the greatest impact.
 With this mindset, the season's changes should feel smoother, but even then, it is okay to miss the sun. I know I do. 
 Avanthi Krishnan is a third year at the Rutgers Business School majoring in finance. Krishnan's column, “RU Uncovered,” runs on alternate Wednesdays.
